newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-Feb US payrolls could validate rate fears.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Feb US payrolls could validate rate fears.

text.p: The February U.S. employment report due on Friday is likely to underline concerns that the U.S. labor market is tight enough to foster potentially inflationary wage gains and to support fears that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates, analysts said.
Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that U.S. non-farm payrolls swelled by 230,000 jobs in February, after payroll growth of 271,000 new jobs in January.
Economists also estimated the unemployment rate fell to 5.3 percent in February from 5.4 percent in January.
Meanwhile, average hourly wages likely rose by 0.4 percent as the average workweek stretched to 34.6 hours from 34.1 hours, economists told Reuters.
Even economists whose payroll growth estimates were below the consensus forecast said the employment picture was too strong for comfort.
John Williams, managing director and chief global markets economist at Bankers Trust, said payroll growth of 175,000 jobs in February would keep the labor market under pressure.
"As Greenspan said, eventually those pressures will show up in prices -- once certain short-term phenomenon have run their course," said Williams.

In his Humphrey-Hawkins Congressional testimony last week, Greenspan mentioned several "temporary factors of uncertain longevity" that were helping to keep inflation in check despite a tight labor market, the most important of them being job insecurity that makes workers hesitate to seek raises. Longer labor union contracts that emphasized job security and involved only modest wage increases and a sharp deceleration in health care costs also restrained the price of labor, he said.
"These are temporary factors that can fade," Williams said. "At some point, the Fed will have to do something "to get the labor market less robust."
Charles Lieberman, chief economist at Chase Securities Inc, estimated that payrolls grew by a strong 275,000 jobs in February as the unemployment rate fell to 5.3 percent.

"Payroll growth should remain quite good, judging by the dearth of layoffs and mild winter weather in the Northeast that should boost construction employment," he said. "The unemployment rate should resume its downward path, though the pace may slow as more people stream into the labor force."

Marilyn Schaja, money market economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, looks for below-consensus payroll growth of 175,000 new jobs in February. Such a figure would "take away some of the pressure for the Fed to (raise rates) in the near term," she said. "It would be status quo for the Fed."

But payroll growth in excess of 200,000 jobs combined with strength in hourly wage gains and workweek length means "you can't rule out a Fed policy change at the March 25 FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee) meeting," Schaja said.
The employment report is scheduled for release at 0830 EST/1330 GMT on Friday, March 7.
